## 1.8.0

- **Provider group memberships are mirrored into the app.** Each sign-in writes the groups the identity provider asserts onto SASjs groups of the same name, so a permission can be granted to a provider group rather than to each of its members. A membership the provider stops asserting is removed at the next sign-in. A name an administrator has already used locally is left alone and reported in the log rather than adopted.
- **The login screen hides the password form** when local sign-in is switched off, which is the default on this package when single sign-on is configured and no break-glass admin is seeded - so the provider's button is the only thing on the screen.
- Upstream v1.8.0.

## 1.7.0

- **The app authenticates users itself.** The `proxyAuth` addon is dropped, so the platform's login wall is no longer in front of the app and a browser user meets one prompt instead of two. The per-app access restriction still decides who may attempt a sign-in, and the app's own group policy decides what they are once they have.
- Local password sign-in is closed by default when single sign-on is configured and no local admin is seeded. Seed `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` for a break-glass local account, which keeps it open.
- Upstream v1.7.0.

## 1.6.0

- **Sign-in is gated on the provider's groups**, by fixed name: `sasjs-admins` signs in as an administrator, `sasjs-users` as an ordinary user, and a user in neither is refused with no account created. The first-user-becomes-administrator bootstrap survives only for providers that cannot express groups at all.
- Upstream v1.6.0.

## 1.5.1

- **The web app only accepts a session it actually returned.** A platform or proxy answering the session route with its own HTML no longer renders the signed-in shell for a user who has no session - which had left such a user with no way to sign in.
- Upstream v1.5.1.

## 1.5.0

- OIDC sign-in sends a PKCE challenge (RFC 7636, S256 method).
- Upstream v1.5.0.

## 1.4.1

- The build authenticates its macro download against the GitHub API, which clears the anonymous rate-limit failures that broke container builds intermittently.
- Upstream v1.4.1.

## 1.4.0

- Local password sign-in can be switched off with `LOCAL_LOGIN_ENABLED=false`.
- Upstream v1.4.0.

## 1.3.7

- Failed password logins are throttled by username, not by IP address: behind a reverse proxy every client shares the proxy's address, so an IP-keyed limit locks out the whole deployment rather than an attacker.
- Upstream v1.3.7.

## 1.3.6

- Every value interpolated into generated stored-program source is escaped, across all four runtimes.
- Upstream v1.3.6.

## 1.3.5

- The session cookie is marked Secure behind a TLS-terminating proxy, where the app itself sees plain http.
- Upstream v1.3.5.

## 1.3.4

- **The configuration is readable without shell access.** Settings live in
  `/app/data/config.env` - the same `KEY=VALUE` format as before, under a
  visible name - and the effective configuration is written to
  `/app/data/config.txt` on every start. `RUN_TIMES`, the auth providers, the
  ports and whether an admin password is set are all visible there; credentials
  appear as `set`/`unset`, never by value.
- **The config file is read, not sourced.** The entrypoint runs as root and the
  data directory is writable by the application user, so executing a file from
  there would let anyone who can write to it run shell as root on the next
  restart - privilege escalation on an application whose purpose is running
  uploaded code. Only `KEY=VALUE` lines are honoured now, with `dotenv`'s
  quoting and comment rules so the entrypoint and the server agree.

## 1.3.3

- **No admin account is created unless you ask for one.** The entrypoint no
  longer generates a password into `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`. With
  `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` unset there is no local admin at all, and the FIRST
  user to sign in through Cloudron SSO becomes the administrator - which makes
  a fresh install usable without hunting for a credential in a dotfile the
  platform's File Manager does not show. Set `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` to seed a
  break-glass local admin instead; a seeded admin counts as an existing
  administrator, so the first SSO user is then a normal user.
- **`/app/data/.env` is the app's configuration file.** It is read on every
  start - by the entrypoint before its defaults, and by the server itself,
  which runs with `DATA_DIR` as its working directory - so the settings above
  can be changed from the File Manager. Cloudron's own addon credentials are
  still read from the environment at every start and are never cached here.
- Upstream: server mode no longer refuses to start without
  `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` when an external provider is enabled, because that
  provider can bootstrap the first administrator. It still fails closed when no
  provider is configured, since then no account could ever exist.

## 1.2.1

- **The Cloudron package has moved into the SASjs Server repository** as
  `container/cloudron/`, and the standalone `sasjs/server-cloudron` repository
  is deprecated. The app package now installs the same container image every
  other user runs - `ghcr.io/sasjs/server`, built and published by the
  repository's own release workflow - so the app version and the image tag
  always refer to the same commit.
- The image entrypoint is platform-neutral: outside Cloudron it is configured
  by the application's own environment variables (with `DATA_DIR` for the
  writable state). Inside Cloudron it detects the `CLOUDRON_*` addon variables
  and wires them up as before; `container/tests/verify-start-sh.sh` keeps both
  sides in sync with the manifest.
- Upstream v1.2.1: the release executables are built with node24 pkg targets,
  and the container image follows the source build on Node 24, which the OIDC
  sign-in path requires.

## 1.1.0

- Upstream v1.1.0, which adds OIDC sign-in and just-in-time provisioning.
- **Cloudron single sign-on replaces LDAP.** The `oidc` addon is declared with
  `loginRedirectUri` `/SASLogon/openid/callback`, `logoutRedirectUri`
  `/SASLogon/openid/logout` and `tokenSignatureAlgorithm` RS256; the `ldap`
  addon is gone. `start.sh` maps `CLOUDRON_OIDC_*` onto the app's `OIDC_*`
  names and builds the absolute `OIDC_REDIRECT_URI` the app requires from
  `CLOUDRON_APP_ORIGIN`. `AUTH_PROVIDERS` still defaults to SSO and an empty
  value falls back to local accounts. Note the single-dash default: `:-` would
  treat an explicitly empty value as unset and re-enable OIDC.
- **The image now builds from source instead of the `linux.zip` release
  asset.** That asset is a `pkg` binary targeting node16, which has no global
  `fetch` - and the OIDC sign-in path calls it. Against the v1.1.0 binary,
  `GET /SASLogon/openid` returns 500 (`Failed to fetch the OIDC discovery
  document ...: undefined is not a function`); the same source built on a
  modern Node completes the sign-in redirect. The Dockerfile clones the pinned
  tag, asserts the commit it resolves to, and builds the web bundle then the
  API, as upstream's own `DockerfileApi` does. Side effect: the unfixable
  findings from the pkg bundle's own Go stdlib and bundled `node_modules` are
  gone.
- `tests/verify-oidc.sh` boots the app with Cloudron-shaped OIDC configuration
  against a stub identity provider and asserts the sign-in route redirects with
  our client id, our exact redirect URI, the openid scope and a state value.
  The CI smoke job runs the same assertion against the built image.
- `tests/verify-start-sh.sh` now also asserts that `OIDC_SIGNING_ALG` matches
  the manifest's `tokenSignatureAlgorithm` and that `loginRedirectUri` matches
  the path `start.sh` builds - a mismatch fails only at sign-in, which is the
  worst place to find it.
- `tests/verify-runtimes.sh` is removed. It exercised the release asset this
  package no longer uses, and its runtime coverage (both runtimes execute) is
  in `verify-server-mode.sh` and the CI smoke job.
- The app-level harnesses take `API_BIN`, skip when no server or MongoDB is
  present, and refuse to run when something already holds their port - a stale
  process makes every assertion describe the old binary.

## 0.39.8

- Initial Cloudron package for SASjs Server v0.39.8.
- Server mode: MongoDB addon for storage, Cloudron LDAP addon for user login,
  local storage for the SASjs Drive and logs.
- Default runtimes are `js,py` (JavaScript and Python stored programs). Node
  comes from the `cloudron/node-base` image, Python 3 is installed in the
  Dockerfile, so the package needs no SAS binary.
- SAS and R remain available by adding them to `RUN_TIMES` and supplying their
  executable paths from outside the image.
- `AUTH_PROVIDERS` can be set to an empty value to disable Cloudron LDAP and
  authenticate against the local database only.
- Initial local admin password generated on first boot into
  `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`.
- CI pipeline (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`): validate, build, Trivy reports
  (full os+library table and SARIF artifact) with gates on OS packages and
  Dockerfile misconfiguration, and a server-mode smoke test against MongoDB 8
  that drives the real auth flow and executes both runtimes. The smoke job
  depends only on validate, so a scan finding cannot hide a functional failure.
- `linux-libc-dev` is pulled up to the archive's current version in the
  Dockerfile, which clears the kernel-header CVEs the OS-layer scan gate would
  otherwise flag on every build.
- start.sh creates the `/app/data` tree before writing the initial admin
  password. On Cloudron the localstorage addon always creates that directory,
  so the ordering bug was invisible there; it broke a plain `docker run` and was
  caught by the CI smoke test. The start.sh harness no longer pre-creates the
  directory, so it covers this.
- `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` is now honoured when supplied. Previously start.sh
  always overwrote it with a generated password, which is why the first CI
  smoke run failed to authenticate. Unset, behaviour is unchanged: a password
  is generated into `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`.
- `.trivyignore.yaml` records one audited exception: `DS-0002` wants a non-root
  `USER`, but Cloudron images must start as root to chown the platform-managed
  `/app/data` before dropping to the `cloudron` user via gosu.
- Manifest: `proxyAuth` puts the whole app behind Cloudron's authentication
  wall, excluding only the health-check endpoint. This replaces the VPN
  requirement: VPN gating has no manifest field (it is the per-app platform
  setting `requiresVpn`), so Cloudron auth is enforced instead.
  `supportsBearerAuth` is enabled so programmatic SASjs clients still reach the
  API through the wall.
- Manifest: `minBoxVersion` raised to 10.0.0 and `targetBoxVersion` set to
  10.0.5, the box this estate runs. `mediaLinks` is populated - Cloudron
  requires it to be non-empty to publish - with a 3:1 banner composed from the
  app's own logo, since upstream ships no screenshots.
- Manifest: `packageUrl`, needed by `cloudron versions init` when publishing.
  This is also what forces `minBoxVersion` to 10.0.0: Cloudron's loader rejects
  the manifest with "manifest.packageUrl requires minBoxVersion of atleast
  10.0.0", a cross-field rule its JSON schema does not express and so does not
  catch. `scripts/check-manifest.py` now enforces these rules - read from the
  schema's own field descriptions - and `tests/verify-manifest.sh` proves it
  reproduces that exact error, so the manifest cannot be published unloadable
  again.
- Release pipeline (`.github/workflows/release.yml`): a `v*` tag matching the
  manifest version builds the image, smoke tests it before pushing anything,
  pushes it to `ghcr.io/sasjs/server-cloudron`, records the digest in
  `CloudronVersions.json`, commits the catalogue back and creates the release.
- `scripts/update-versions.py` generates and validates `CloudronVersions.json`,
  because Cloudron's `cloudron versions add` needs the CLI and a logged-in
  workstation. It inlines `file://` text fields, keeps `icon` as a reference,
  refuses to move semver backwards, and refuses a manifest missing any field
  Cloudron requires for publishing.
- A recorded catalogue entry is refreshed whenever anything about it changes,
  not only when the image digest changes. The guard previously compared the
  image alone, so a manifest-only fix - a corrected `minBoxVersion`, say -
  would leave the catalogue serving the stale embedded manifest and installs
  would keep failing on a manifest that no longer existed in the repository.
- The smoke test moved to `.github/actions/smoke-test` so CI and the release
  workflow share one implementation.
- Manifest: `memoryLimit` set to 1 GiB. Cloudron's default is 256 MB, which
  this app exceeds - it runs Node, serves the web UI from the same process and
  spawns a `node` or `python3` child per stored program.
- Manifest: `postInstallMessage` (`file://POSTINSTALL.md`) and a `checklist`
  covering the initial admin password and the Drive-write trust boundary, plus
  `iconUrl` and `documentationUrl` for the community app listing.
- Dockerfile: `EXPOSE 5000`, matching the manifest's `httpPort`.
- `scripts/verify-installable.py` checks, using only anonymous requests, that a
  Cloudron box can actually install the package: it fetches the published
  catalogue, confirms the registry serves the exact digest the catalogue names
  (not merely an image with the right tag), and fetches every URL the dashboard
  and store will. It fails loudly if any step needs a credential, which is the
  difference between "the pipeline is green" and "a box can install this".
- Verification harnesses in `tests/`: start.sh behaviour (33 assertions),
  desktop-mode runtimes, server mode against MongoDB (9 assertions), manifest
  rules, and the catalogue generator.

manifest.description:
# SASjs Server

SASjs Server is an open-source Node.js wrapper that gives you a REST API, a
filesystem (SASjs Drive) for storing programs, execution of Stored Programs
from a URL, and web-app streaming - the same role SAS 9 Stored Processes and
Viya Jobs play.

This package runs it in **server mode**: multi-user, with Cloudron single
sign-on, and a MongoDB store.

## Runtimes: JavaScript and Python

`RUN_TIMES` defaults to `js,py`, so stored programs are JavaScript or Python.
Node and Python 3 are both in the image, which makes this package
self-contained - **no SAS binary is required**.

SAS and R can be enabled by adding them to `RUN_TIMES`, but each needs an
executable supplied from outside the image: SAS is proprietary and licensed
and cannot be redistributed, and R is not installed here.

## Addons used

- **MongoDB** - the server-mode database (users, groups, tokens, sessions).
- **OIDC** - Cloudron single sign-on. Users sign in with their Cloudron
  account, so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without
  maintaining a second account list.
- **Local storage** - `/app/data`, which holds the SASjs Drive, logs, uploads
  and the initial admin password.

## Authentication

The app authenticates users itself, through Cloudron single sign-on (OIDC), so
access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without maintaining a second
account list. There is no platform login wall in front of it: the app's own
sign-in screen is what a visitor meets.

Sign-in requires group membership, by fixed name. Create both groups under
**Users > Groups** and assign people to them:

- `sasjs-users` - everyone who should use the app; members are ordinary users.
- `sasjs-admins` - its administrators.

A user in neither group is refused at sign-in. Membership of `sasjs-admins` is
what makes a SASjs administrator - nobody becomes one simply by signing in
first. Set `AUTH_PROVIDERS` to an empty value to skip SSO and authenticate
against the local database only.

Password sign-in for local accounts is closed by default while single sign-on
is configured: no local account exists unless one is seeded, and an exposed
password form is the one credential an anonymous caller can guess. To seed a
break-glass local `admin` account, put `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong
password>` in `/app/data/config.env` and restart the app - seeding one keeps
password sign-in open, which is the point of a break-glass account. Set
`LOCAL_LOGIN_ENABLED` explicitly to override either default.

## Access control

Restrict the app to the users and groups who should reach it, before anyone
signs in: open the app's **Settings > Access control** and choose "Only allow
the following users and groups". A Cloudron install is unrestricted by default,
which here means every Cloudron user can reach the sign-in screen and try -
and the `js` and `py` runtimes execute whatever is uploaded to SASjs Drive, so
the app itself is a privilege boundary worth closing.

## Configuration

Settings live in `/app/data/config.env` (visible in the File Manager; `.env` in
the same directory still works, and `config.env` wins where both set a key).
The effective configuration - runtimes, ports, which auth providers are on,
whether the admin password is set - is written to `/app/data/config.txt` on
every start, so it can be read without opening a terminal.

## A note on what these runtimes do

The `js` and `py` runtimes execute the program files stored on SASjs Drive,
server-side. That is the point of the application - and it is a privilege
boundary. Anyone who can write to the Drive can run code in this container.

Keep the app behind Cloudron access control, and grant Drive write access only
to trusted authors.

## Backups

Cloudron backs up `/app/data` and the MongoDB addon, so the SASjs Drive, logs
and uploaded content are all covered. Backups are taken automatically before
every app update.
manifest.postInstallMessage:
### SASjs Server is running

**Create the groups before anyone signs in.** Sign-in depends on group
membership: under **Users > Groups** create `sasjs-users` for everyone who
should use the app and `sasjs-admins` for its administrators, then assign people
to them. A user in neither group is refused at sign-in, and membership of
`sasjs-admins` is what makes a SASjs administrator - nobody becomes one by
signing in first. Both groups appear inside the app as well, so permissions can
be granted to the group instead of user by user; membership is taken from
Cloudron at each sign-in, and cannot be edited in the app.

**Restrict access as well.** Open the app's **Settings > Access control** and
choose "Only allow the following users and groups". The app authenticates users
itself through Cloudron single sign-on, so this is what decides who can even
attempt to sign in.

**Sign in with Cloudron.** The app shows its own sign-in screen; use "Sign in
with Cloudron". Once you are in, grant other users what they need under
Settings > Permissions.

**Break-glass local account (optional).** To seed a local `admin` account, add
`ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong password>` to `/app/data/config.env` (File
Manager, or this app's Terminal) and restart the app. Seeding one keeps password
sign-in open, which is the point of a break-glass account; password sign-in is
otherwise closed while single sign-on is configured.

**Stored programs execute real code.** The `js` and `py` runtimes run whatever
is uploaded to SASjs Drive, server-side. Grant Drive write access only to
trusted authors, and keep this app behind Cloudron access control.

**Check it is up.**

```
curl $CLOUDRON-APP-ORIGIN/SASjsApi/info
```

**No SAS binary is required.** JavaScript and Python are built into the image.
SAS and R are available if you add them to `RUN_TIMES` and point `SAS_PATH` or
`R_PATH` at an executable you supply - SAS is licensed and is not
redistributed here.

Full notes, including the CI pipeline and what was verified, are in the
repository README.

- **The login screen hides the password form** when local sign-in is switched off, which is the default on this package when single sign-on is configured and no break-glass admin is seeded - so the provider's button is the only thing on the screen.
- Upstream v1.8.0.

## 1.7.0

- **The app authenticates users itself.** The `proxyAuth` addon is dropped, so the platform's login wall is no longer in front of the app and a browser user meets one prompt instead of two. The per-app access restriction still decides who may attempt a sign-in, and the app's own group policy decides what they are once they have.
- Local password sign-in is closed by default when single sign-on is configured and no local admin is seeded. Seed `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` for a break-glass local account, which keeps it open.
- Upstream v1.7.0.

## 1.6.0

- **Sign-in is gated on the provider's groups**, by fixed name: `sasjs-admins` signs in as an administrator, `sasjs-users` as an ordinary user, and a user in neither is refused with no account created. The first-user-becomes-administrator bootstrap survives only for providers that cannot express groups at all.
- Upstream v1.6.0.

## 1.5.1

- **The web app only accepts a session it actually returned.** A platform or proxy answering the session route with its own HTML no longer renders the signed-in shell for a user who has no session - which had left such a user with no way to sign in.
- Upstream v1.5.1.

## 1.5.0

- OIDC sign-in sends a PKCE challenge (RFC 7636, S256 method).
- Upstream v1.5.0.

## 1.4.1

- The build authenticates its macro download against the GitHub API, which clears the anonymous rate-limit failures that broke container builds intermittently.
- Upstream v1.4.1.

## 1.4.0

- Local password sign-in can be switched off with `LOCAL_LOGIN_ENABLED=false`.
- Upstream v1.4.0.

## 1.3.7

- Failed password logins are throttled by username, not by IP address: behind a reverse proxy every client shares the proxy's address, so an IP-keyed limit locks out the whole deployment rather than an attacker.
- Upstream v1.3.7.

## 1.3.6

- Every value interpolated into generated stored-program source is escaped, across all four runtimes.
- Upstream v1.3.6.

## 1.3.5

- The session cookie is marked Secure behind a TLS-terminating proxy, where the app itself sees plain http.
- Upstream v1.3.5.

## 1.3.4

- **The configuration is readable without shell access.** Settings live in
  `/app/data/config.env` - the same `KEY=VALUE` format as before, under a
  visible name - and the effective configuration is written to
  `/app/data/config.txt` on every start. `RUN_TIMES`, the auth providers, the
  ports and whether an admin password is set are all visible there; credentials
  appear as `set`/`unset`, never by value.
- **The config file is read, not sourced.** The entrypoint runs as root and the
  data directory is writable by the application user, so executing a file from
  there would let anyone who can write to it run shell as root on the next
  restart - privilege escalation on an application whose purpose is running
  uploaded code. Only `KEY=VALUE` lines are honoured now, with `dotenv`'s
  quoting and comment rules so the entrypoint and the server agree.

## 1.3.3

- **No admin account is created unless you ask for one.** The entrypoint no
  longer generates a password into `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`. With
  `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` unset there is no local admin at all, and the FIRST
  user to sign in through Cloudron SSO becomes the administrator - which makes
  a fresh install usable without hunting for a credential in a dotfile the
  platform's File Manager does not show. Set `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` to seed a
  break-glass local admin instead; a seeded admin counts as an existing
  administrator, so the first SSO user is then a normal user.
- **`/app/data/.env` is the app's configuration file.** It is read on every
  start - by the entrypoint before its defaults, and by the server itself,
  which runs with `DATA_DIR` as its working directory - so the settings above
  can be changed from the File Manager. Cloudron's own addon credentials are
  still read from the environment at every start and are never cached here.
- Upstream: server mode no longer refuses to start without
  `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` when an external provider is enabled, because that
  provider can bootstrap the first administrator. It still fails closed when no
  provider is configured, since then no account could ever exist.

## 1.2.1

- **The Cloudron package has moved into the SASjs Server repository** as
  `container/cloudron/`, and the standalone `sasjs/server-cloudron` repository
  is deprecated. The app package now installs the same container image every
  other user runs - `ghcr.io/sasjs/server`, built and published by the
  repository's own release workflow - so the app version and the image tag
  always refer to the same commit.
- The image entrypoint is platform-neutral: outside Cloudron it is configured
  by the application's own environment variables (with `DATA_DIR` for the
  writable state). Inside Cloudron it detects the `CLOUDRON_*` addon variables
  and wires them up as before; `container/tests/verify-start-sh.sh` keeps both
  sides in sync with the manifest.
- Upstream v1.2.1: the release executables are built with node24 pkg targets,
  and the container image follows the source build on Node 24, which the OIDC
  sign-in path requires.

## 1.1.0

- Upstream v1.1.0, which adds OIDC sign-in and just-in-time provisioning.
- **Cloudron single sign-on replaces LDAP.** The `oidc` addon is declared with
  `loginRedirectUri` `/SASLogon/openid/callback`, `logoutRedirectUri`
  `/SASLogon/openid/logout` and `tokenSignatureAlgorithm` RS256; the `ldap`
  addon is gone. `start.sh` maps `CLOUDRON_OIDC_*` onto the app's `OIDC_*`
  names and builds the absolute `OIDC_REDIRECT_URI` the app requires from
  `CLOUDRON_APP_ORIGIN`. `AUTH_PROVIDERS` still defaults to SSO and an empty
  value falls back to local accounts. Note the single-dash default: `:-` would
  treat an explicitly empty value as unset and re-enable OIDC.
- **The image now builds from source instead of the `linux.zip` release
  asset.** That asset is a `pkg` binary targeting node16, which has no global
  `fetch` - and the OIDC sign-in path calls it. Against the v1.1.0 binary,
  `GET /SASLogon/openid` returns 500 (`Failed to fetch the OIDC discovery
  document ...: undefined is not a function`); the same source built on a
  modern Node completes the sign-in redirect. The Dockerfile clones the pinned
  tag, asserts the commit it resolves to, and builds the web bundle then the
  API, as upstream's own `DockerfileApi` does. Side effect: the unfixable
  findings from the pkg bundle's own Go stdlib and bundled `node_modules` are
  gone.
- `tests/verify-oidc.sh` boots the app with Cloudron-shaped OIDC configuration
  against a stub identity provider and asserts the sign-in route redirects with
  our client id, our exact redirect URI, the openid scope and a state value.
  The CI smoke job runs the same assertion against the built image.
- `tests/verify-start-sh.sh` now also asserts that `OIDC_SIGNING_ALG` matches
  the manifest's `tokenSignatureAlgorithm` and that `loginRedirectUri` matches
  the path `start.sh` builds - a mismatch fails only at sign-in, which is the
  worst place to find it.
- `tests/verify-runtimes.sh` is removed. It exercised the release asset this
  package no longer uses, and its runtime coverage (both runtimes execute) is
  in `verify-server-mode.sh` and the CI smoke job.
- The app-level harnesses take `API_BIN`, skip when no server or MongoDB is
  present, and refuse to run when something already holds their port - a stale
  process makes every assertion describe the old binary.

## 0.39.8

- Initial Cloudron package for SASjs Server v0.39.8.
- Server mode: MongoDB addon for storage, Cloudron LDAP addon for user login,
  local storage for the SASjs Drive and logs.
- Default runtimes are `js,py` (JavaScript and Python stored programs). Node
  comes from the `cloudron/node-base` image, Python 3 is installed in the
  Dockerfile, so the package needs no SAS binary.
- SAS and R remain available by adding them to `RUN_TIMES` and supplying their
  executable paths from outside the image.
- `AUTH_PROVIDERS` can be set to an empty value to disable Cloudron LDAP and
  authenticate against the local database only.
- Initial local admin password generated on first boot into
  `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`.
- CI pipeline (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`): validate, build, Trivy reports
  (full os+library table and SARIF artifact) with gates on OS packages and
  Dockerfile misconfiguration, and a server-mode smoke test against MongoDB 8
  that drives the real auth flow and executes both runtimes. The smoke job
  depends only on validate, so a scan finding cannot hide a functional failure.
- `linux-libc-dev` is pulled up to the archive's current version in the
  Dockerfile, which clears the kernel-header CVEs the OS-layer scan gate would
  otherwise flag on every build.
- start.sh creates the `/app/data` tree before writing the initial admin
  password. On Cloudron the localstorage addon always creates that directory,
  so the ordering bug was invisible there; it broke a plain `docker run` and was
  caught by the CI smoke test. The start.sh harness no longer pre-creates the
  directory, so it covers this.
- `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` is now honoured when supplied. Previously start.sh
  always overwrote it with a generated password, which is why the first CI
  smoke run failed to authenticate. Unset, behaviour is unchanged: a password
  is generated into `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`.
- `.trivyignore.yaml` records one audited exception: `DS-0002` wants a non-root
  `USER`, but Cloudron images must start as root to chown the platform-managed
  `/app/data` before dropping to the `cloudron` user via gosu.
- Manifest: `proxyAuth` puts the whole app behind Cloudron's authentication
  wall, excluding only the health-check endpoint. This replaces the VPN
  requirement: VPN gating has no manifest field (it is the per-app platform
  setting `requiresVpn`), so Cloudron auth is enforced instead.
  `supportsBearerAuth` is enabled so programmatic SASjs clients still reach the
  API through the wall.
- Manifest: `minBoxVersion` raised to 10.0.0 and `targetBoxVersion` set to
  10.0.5, the box this estate runs. `mediaLinks` is populated - Cloudron
  requires it to be non-empty to publish - with a 3:1 banner composed from the
  app's own logo, since upstream ships no screenshots.
- Manifest: `packageUrl`, needed by `cloudron versions init` when publishing.
  This is also what forces `minBoxVersion` to 10.0.0: Cloudron's loader rejects
  the manifest with "manifest.packageUrl requires minBoxVersion of atleast
  10.0.0", a cross-field rule its JSON schema does not express and so does not
  catch. `scripts/check-manifest.py` now enforces these rules - read from the
  schema's own field descriptions - and `tests/verify-manifest.sh` proves it
  reproduces that exact error, so the manifest cannot be published unloadable
  again.
- Release pipeline (`.github/workflows/release.yml`): a `v*` tag matching the
  manifest version builds the image, smoke tests it before pushing anything,
  pushes it to `ghcr.io/sasjs/server-cloudron`, records the digest in
  `CloudronVersions.json`, commits the catalogue back and creates the release.
- `scripts/update-versions.py` generates and validates `CloudronVersions.json`,
  because Cloudron's `cloudron versions add` needs the CLI and a logged-in
  workstation. It inlines `file://` text fields, keeps `icon` as a reference,
  refuses to move semver backwards, and refuses a manifest missing any field
  Cloudron requires for publishing.
- A recorded catalogue entry is refreshed whenever anything about it changes,
  not only when the image digest changes. The guard previously compared the
  image alone, so a manifest-only fix - a corrected `minBoxVersion`, say -
  would leave the catalogue serving the stale embedded manifest and installs
  would keep failing on a manifest that no longer existed in the repository.
- The smoke test moved to `.github/actions/smoke-test` so CI and the release
  workflow share one implementation.
- Manifest: `memoryLimit` set to 1 GiB. Cloudron's default is 256 MB, which
  this app exceeds - it runs Node, serves the web UI from the same process and
  spawns a `node` or `python3` child per stored program.
- Manifest: `postInstallMessage` (`file://POSTINSTALL.md`) and a `checklist`
  covering the initial admin password and the Drive-write trust boundary, plus
  `iconUrl` and `documentationUrl` for the community app listing.
- Dockerfile: `EXPOSE 5000`, matching the manifest's `httpPort`.
- `scripts/verify-installable.py` checks, using only anonymous requests, that a
  Cloudron box can actually install the package: it fetches the published
  catalogue, confirms the registry serves the exact digest the catalogue names
  (not merely an image with the right tag), and fetches every URL the dashboard
  and store will. It fails loudly if any step needs a credential, which is the
  difference between "the pipeline is green" and "a box can install this".
- Verification harnesses in `tests/`: start.sh behaviour (33 assertions),
  desktop-mode runtimes, server mode against MongoDB (9 assertions), manifest
  rules, and the catalogue generator.

manifest.description:
# SASjs Server

SASjs Server is an open-source Node.js wrapper that gives you a REST API, a
filesystem (SASjs Drive) for storing programs, execution of Stored Programs
from a URL, and web-app streaming - the same role SAS 9 Stored Processes and
Viya Jobs play.

This package runs it in **server mode**: multi-user, with Cloudron single
sign-on, and a MongoDB store.

## Runtimes: JavaScript and Python

`RUN_TIMES` defaults to `js,py`, so stored programs are JavaScript or Python.
Node and Python 3 are both in the image, which makes this package
self-contained - **no SAS binary is required**.

SAS and R can be enabled by adding them to `RUN_TIMES`, but each needs an
executable supplied from outside the image: SAS is proprietary and licensed
and cannot be redistributed, and R is not installed here.

## Addons used

- **MongoDB** - the server-mode database (users, groups, tokens, sessions).
- **OIDC** - Cloudron single sign-on. Users sign in with their Cloudron
  account, so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without
  maintaining a second account list.
- **Local storage** - `/app/data`, which holds the SASjs Drive, logs, uploads
  and the initial admin password.

## Authentication

The app authenticates users itself, through Cloudron single sign-on (OIDC), so
access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without maintaining a second
account list. There is no platform login wall in front of it: the app's own
sign-in screen is what a visitor meets.

Sign-in requires group membership, by fixed name. Create both groups under
**Users > Groups** and assign people to them:

- `sasjs-users` - everyone who should use the app; members are ordinary users.
- `sasjs-admins` - its administrators.

A user in neither group is refused at sign-in. Membership of `sasjs-admins` is
what makes a SASjs administrator - nobody becomes one simply by signing in
first. Set `AUTH_PROVIDERS` to an empty value to skip SSO and authenticate
against the local database only.

Password sign-in for local accounts is closed by default while single sign-on
is configured: no local account exists unless one is seeded, and an exposed
password form is the one credential an anonymous caller can guess. To seed a
break-glass local `admin` account, put `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong
password>` in `/app/data/config.env` and restart the app - seeding one keeps
password sign-in open, which is the point of a break-glass account. Set
`LOCAL_LOGIN_ENABLED` explicitly to override either default.

## Access control

Restrict the app to the users and groups who should reach it, before anyone
signs in: open the app's **Settings > Access control** and choose "Only allow
the following users and groups". A Cloudron install is unrestricted by default,
which here means every Cloudron user can reach the sign-in screen and try -
and the `js` and `py` runtimes execute whatever is uploaded to SASjs Drive, so
the app itself is a privilege boundary worth closing.

## Configuration

Settings live in `/app/data/config.env` (visible in the File Manager; `.env` in
the same directory still works, and `config.env` wins where both set a key).
The effective configuration - runtimes, ports, which auth providers are on,
whether the admin password is set - is written to `/app/data/config.txt` on
every start, so it can be read without opening a terminal.

## A note on what these runtimes do

The `js` and `py` runtimes execute the program files stored on SASjs Drive,
server-side. That is the point of the application - and it is a privilege
boundary. Anyone who can write to the Drive can run code in this container.

Keep the app behind Cloudron access control, and grant Drive write access only
to trusted authors.

## Backups

Cloudron backs up `/app/data` and the MongoDB addon, so the SASjs Drive, logs
and uploaded content are all covered. Backups are taken automatically before
every app update.
manifest.postInstallMessage:
### SASjs Server is running

**Create the groups before anyone signs in.** Sign-in depends on group
membership: under **Users > Groups** create `sasjs-users` for everyone who
should use the app and `sasjs-admins` for its administrators, then assign people
to them. A user in neither group is refused at sign-in, and membership of
`sasjs-admins` is what makes a SASjs administrator - nobody becomes one by
signing in first. Both groups appear inside the app as well, so permissions can
be granted to the group instead of user by user; membership is taken from
Cloudron at each sign-in, and cannot be edited in the app.

**Restrict access as well.** Open the app's **Settings > Access control** and
choose "Only allow the following users and groups". The app authenticates users
itself through Cloudron single sign-on, so this is what decides who can even
attempt to sign in.

**Sign in with Cloudron.** The app shows its own sign-in screen; use "Sign in
with Cloudron". Once you are in, grant other users what they need under
Settings > Permissions.

**Break-glass local account (optional).** To seed a local `admin` account, add
`ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong password>` to `/app/data/config.env` (File
Manager, or this app's Terminal) and restart the app. Seeding one keeps password
sign-in open, which is the point of a break-glass account; password sign-in is
otherwise closed while single sign-on is configured.

**Stored programs execute real code.** The `js` and `py` runtimes run whatever
is uploaded to SASjs Drive, server-side. Grant Drive write access only to
trusted authors, and keep this app behind Cloudron access control.

**Check it is up.**

```
curl $CLOUDRON-APP-ORIGIN/SASjsApi/info
```

**No SAS binary is required.** JavaScript and Python are built into the image.
SAS and R are available if you add them to `RUN_TIMES` and point `SAS_PATH` or
`R_PATH` at an executable you supply - SAS is licensed and is not
redistributed here.

Full notes, including the CI pipeline and what was verified, are in the
repository README.

  there would let anyone who can write to it run shell as root on the next
  restart - privilege escalation on an application whose purpose is running
  uploaded code. Only `KEY=VALUE` lines are honoured now, with `dotenv`'s

  longer generates a password into `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`. With

  user to sign in through Cloudron SSO becomes the administrator - which makes
  a fresh install usable without hunting for a credential in a dotfile the
  platform's File Manager does not show. Set `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` to seed a
  break-glass local admin instead; a seeded admin counts as an existing
  administrator, so the first SSO user is then a normal user.

  start - by the entrypoint before its defaults, and by the server itself,
  which runs with `DATA_DIR` as its working directory - so the settings above
  can be changed from the File Manager. Cloudron's own addon credentials are
  still read from the environment at every start and are never cached here.

  `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` when an external provider is enabled, because that
  provider can bootstrap the first administrator. It still fails closed when no
  provider is configured, since then no account could ever exist.

  by the application's own environment variables (with `DATA_DIR` for the
  writable state). Inside Cloudron it detects the `CLOUDRON_*` addon variables
  and wires them up as before; `container/tests/verify-start-sh.sh` keeps both

  and the container image follows the source build on Node 24, which the OIDC
  sign-in path requires.

- **Cloudron single sign-on replaces LDAP.** The `oidc` addon is declared with

  API, as upstream's own `DockerfileApi` does. Side effect: the unfixable

- Initial Cloudron package for SASjs Server v0.39.8.
- Server mode: MongoDB addon for storage, Cloudron LDAP addon for user login,
  local storage for the SASjs Drive and logs.
- Default runtimes are `js,py` (JavaScript and Python stored programs). Node

  executable paths from outside the image.
- `AUTH_PROVIDERS` can be set to an empty value to disable Cloudron LDAP and

  Dockerfile misconfiguration, and a server-mode smoke test against MongoDB 8
  that drives the real auth flow and executes both runtimes. The smoke job

  `USER`, but Cloudron images must start as root to chown the platform-managed
  `/app/data` before dropping to the `cloudron` user via gosu.

  wall, excluding only the health-check endpoint. This replaces the VPN
  requirement: VPN gating has no manifest field (it is the per-app platform
  setting `requiresVpn`), so Cloudron auth is enforced instead.

  API through the wall.

  10.0.5, the box this estate runs. `mediaLinks` is populated - Cloudron
  requires it to be non-empty to publish - with a 3:1 banner composed from the
  app's own logo, since upstream ships no screenshots.

  This is also what forces `minBoxVersion` to 10.0.0: Cloudron's loader rejects
  the manifest with "manifest.packageUrl requires minBoxVersion of atleast
  10.0.0", a cross-field rule its JSON schema does not express and so does not
  catch. `scripts/check-manifest.py` now enforces these rules - read from the
  schema's own field descriptions - and `tests/verify-manifest.sh` proves it
  reproduces that exact error, so the manifest cannot be published unloadable
  again.

  manifest version builds the image, smoke tests it before pushing anything,
  pushes it to `ghcr.io/sasjs/server-cloudron`, records the digest in
  `CloudronVersions.json`, commits the catalogue back and creates the release.

  because Cloudron's `cloudron versions add` needs the CLI and a logged-in
  workstation. It inlines `file://` text fields, keeps `icon` as a reference,
  refuses to move semver backwards, and refuses a manifest missing any field
  Cloudron requires for publishing.

  not only when the image digest changes. The guard previously compared the
  image alone, so a manifest-only fix - a corrected `minBoxVersion`, say -
  would leave the catalogue serving the stale embedded manifest and installs
  would keep failing on a manifest that no longer existed in the repository.

  workflow share one implementation.
- Manifest: `memoryLimit` set to 1 GiB. Cloudron's default is 256 MB, which
  this app exceeds - it runs Node, serves the web UI from the same process and
  spawns a `node` or `python3` child per stored program.
- Manifest: `postInstallMessage` (`file://POSTINSTALL.md`) and a `checklist`
  covering the initial admin password and the Drive-write trust boundary, plus
  `iconUrl` and `documentationUrl` for the community app listing.
- Dockerfile: `EXPOSE 5000`, matching the manifest's `httpPort`.
- `scripts/verify-installable.py` checks, using only anonymous requests, that a
  Cloudron box can actually install the package: it fetches the published
  catalogue, confirms the registry serves the exact digest the catalogue names
  (not merely an image with the right tag), and fetches every URL the dashboard
  and store will. It fails loudly if any step needs a credential, which is the
  difference between "the pipeline is green" and "a box can install this".
- Verification harnesses in `tests/`: start.sh behaviour (33 assertions),
  desktop-mode runtimes, server mode against MongoDB (9 assertions), manifest
  rules, and the catalogue generator.

manifest.description:
# SASjs Server

SASjs Server is an open-source Node.js wrapper that gives you a REST API, a
filesystem (SASjs Drive) for storing programs, execution of Stored Programs
from a URL, and web-app streaming - the same role SAS 9 Stored Processes and
Viya Jobs play.

This package runs it in **server mode**: multi-user, with Cloudron single
sign-on, and a MongoDB store.

## Runtimes: JavaScript and Python

`RUN_TIMES` defaults to `js,py`, so stored programs are JavaScript or Python.
Node and Python 3 are both in the image, which makes this package
self-contained - **no SAS binary is required**.

SAS and R can be enabled by adding them to `RUN_TIMES`, but each needs an
executable supplied from outside the image: SAS is proprietary and licensed
and cannot be redistributed, and R is not installed here.

## Addons used

- **MongoDB** - the server-mode database (users, groups, tokens, sessions).
- **OIDC** - Cloudron single sign-on. Users sign in with their Cloudron
  account, so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without
  maintaining a second account list.
- **Local storage** - `/app/data`, which holds the SASjs Drive, logs, uploads
  and the initial admin password.

## Authentication

The app authenticates users itself, through Cloudron single sign-on (OIDC), so
access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without maintaining a second
account list. There is no platform login wall in front of it: the app's own
sign-in screen is what a visitor meets.

Sign-in requires group membership, by fixed name. Create both groups under
**Users > Groups** and assign people to them:

- `sasjs-users` - everyone who should use the app; members are ordinary users.
- `sasjs-admins` - its administrators.

A user in neither group is refused at sign-in. Membership of `sasjs-admins` is
what makes a SASjs administrator - nobody becomes one simply by signing in
first. Set `AUTH_PROVIDERS` to an empty value to skip SSO and authenticate
against the local database only.

Password sign-in for local accounts is closed by default while single sign-on
is configured: no local account exists unless one is seeded, and an exposed
password form is the one credential an anonymous caller can guess. To seed a
break-glass local `admin` account, put `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong
password>` in `/app/data/config.env` and restart the app - seeding one keeps
password sign-in open, which is the point of a break-glass account. Set
`LOCAL_LOGIN_ENABLED` explicitly to override either default.

## Access control

Restrict the app to the users and groups who should reach it, before anyone
signs in: open the app's **Settings > Access control** and choose "Only allow
the following users and groups". A Cloudron install is unrestricted by default,
which here means every Cloudron user can reach the sign-in screen and try -
and the `js` and `py` runtimes execute whatever is uploaded to SASjs Drive, so
the app itself is a privilege boundary worth closing.

## Configuration

Settings live in `/app/data/config.env` (visible in the File Manager; `.env` in
the same directory still works, and `config.env` wins where both set a key).
The effective configuration - runtimes, ports, which auth providers are on,
whether the admin password is set - is written to `/app/data/config.txt` on
every start, so it can be read without opening a terminal.

## A note on what these runtimes do

The `js` and `py` runtimes execute the program files stored on SASjs Drive,
server-side. That is the point of the application - and it is a privilege
boundary. Anyone who can write to the Drive can run code in this container.

Keep the app behind Cloudron access control, and grant Drive write access only
to trusted authors.

## Backups

Cloudron backs up `/app/data` and the MongoDB addon, so the SASjs Drive, logs
and uploaded content are all covered. Backups are taken automatically before
every app update.
manifest.postInstallMessage:
### SASjs Server is running

**Create the groups before anyone signs in.** Sign-in depends on group
membership: under **Users > Groups** create `sasjs-users` for everyone who
should use the app and `sasjs-admins` for its administrators, then assign people
to them. A user in neither group is refused at sign-in, and membership of
`sasjs-admins` is what makes a SASjs administrator - nobody becomes one by
signing in first. Both groups appear inside the app as well, so permissions can
be granted to the group instead of user by user; membership is taken from
Cloudron at each sign-in, and cannot be edited in the app.

**Restrict access as well.** Open the app's **Settings > Access control** and
choose "Only allow the following users and groups". The app authenticates users
itself through Cloudron single sign-on, so this is what decides who can even
attempt to sign in.

**Sign in with Cloudron.** The app shows its own sign-in screen; use "Sign in
with Cloudron". Once you are in, grant other users what they need under
Settings > Permissions.

**Break-glass local account (optional).** To seed a local `admin` account, add
`ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong password>` to `/app/data/config.env` (File
Manager, or this app's Terminal) and restart the app. Seeding one keeps password
sign-in open, which is the point of a break-glass account; password sign-in is
otherwise closed while single sign-on is configured.

**Stored programs execute real code.** The `js` and `py` runtimes run whatever
is uploaded to SASjs Drive, server-side. Grant Drive write access only to
trusted authors, and keep this app behind Cloudron access control.

**Check it is up.**

```
curl $CLOUDRON-APP-ORIGIN/SASjsApi/info
```

**No SAS binary is required.** JavaScript and Python are built into the image.
SAS and R are available if you add them to `RUN_TIMES` and point `SAS_PATH` or
`R_PATH` at an executable you supply - SAS is licensed and is not
redistributed here.

Full notes, including the CI pipeline and what was verified, are in the
repository README.

manifest.description:
# SASjs Server

SASjs Server is an open-source Node.js wrapper that gives you a REST API, a
filesystem (SASjs Drive) for storing programs, execution of Stored Programs
from a URL, and web-app streaming - the same role SAS 9 Stored Processes and
Viya Jobs play.

This package runs it in **server mode**: multi-user, with Cloudron single
sign-on, and a MongoDB store.

## Runtimes: JavaScript and Python

`RUN_TIMES` defaults to `js,py`, so stored programs are JavaScript or Python.
Node and Python 3 are both in the image, which makes this package
self-contained - **no SAS binary is required**.

SAS and R can be enabled by adding them to `RUN_TIMES`, but each needs an
executable supplied from outside the image: SAS is proprietary and licensed
and cannot be redistributed, and R is not installed here.

## Addons used

- **MongoDB** - the server-mode database (users, groups, tokens, sessions).
- **OIDC** - Cloudron single sign-on. Users sign in with their Cloudron
  account, so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without
  maintaining a second account list.
- **Local storage** - `/app/data`, which holds the SASjs Drive, logs, uploads
  and the initial admin password.

## Authentication

The app sits behind Cloudron's own authentication wall, so an unauthenticated
visitor gets a Cloudron login screen rather than the application. Set this up
at install time - the `proxyAuth` addon cannot be added to an app afterwards.

Inside that wall, day-to-day logins go through Cloudron single sign-on (OIDC),
so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA. Set `AUTH_PROVIDERS` to an
empty value to skip SSO and authenticate against the local database only.

There is no pre-created admin account. The FIRST user to sign in becomes the
administrator; every user after that is a normal user, so grant the others what
they need under Settings > Permissions once you are in.

A break-glass local `admin` account is optional. To seed one, put
`ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong password>` in `/app/data/.env` (File Manager,
or this app's Terminal) and restart the app. Note that a seeded admin counts as
an existing administrator, so the first SSO user would then be a normal user -
set it before anyone signs in only if that is the arrangement you want.

## A note on what these runtimes do

The `js` and `py` runtimes execute the program files stored on SASjs Drive,
server-side. That is the point of the application - and it is a privilege
boundary. Anyone who can write to the Drive can run code in this container.

Keep the app behind Cloudron access control, and grant Drive write access only
to trusted authors.

## Backups

Cloudron backs up `/app/data` and the MongoDB addon, so the SASjs Drive, logs
and uploaded content are all covered. Backups are taken automatically before
every app update.

manifest.description:
# SASjs Server

SASjs Server is an open-source Node.js wrapper that gives you a REST API, a
filesystem (SASjs Drive) for storing programs, execution of Stored Programs
from a URL, and web-app streaming - the same role SAS 9 Stored Processes and
Viya Jobs play.

This package runs it in **server mode**: multi-user, with Cloudron single
sign-on, and a MongoDB store.

## Runtimes: JavaScript and Python

`RUN_TIMES` defaults to `js,py`, so stored programs are JavaScript or Python.
Node and Python 3 are both in the image, which makes this package
self-contained - **no SAS binary is required**.

SAS and R can be enabled by adding them to `RUN_TIMES`, but each needs an
executable supplied from outside the image: SAS is proprietary and licensed
and cannot be redistributed, and R is not installed here.

## Addons used

- **MongoDB** - the server-mode database (users, groups, tokens, sessions).
- **OIDC** - Cloudron single sign-on. Users sign in with their Cloudron
  account, so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without
  maintaining a second account list.
- **Local storage** - `/app/data`, which holds the SASjs Drive, logs, uploads
  and the initial admin password.

## Authentication

The app sits behind Cloudron's own authentication wall, so an unauthenticated
visitor gets a Cloudron login screen rather than the application. Set this up
at install time - the `proxyAuth` addon cannot be added to an app afterwards.

Inside that wall, day-to-day logins go through Cloudron single sign-on (OIDC),
so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA. Set `AUTH_PROVIDERS` to an
empty value to skip SSO and authenticate against the local database only.

There is no pre-created admin account. The FIRST user to sign in becomes the
administrator; every user after that is a normal user, so grant the others what
they need under Settings > Permissions once you are in.

A break-glass local `admin` account is optional. To seed one, put
`ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong password>` in `/app/data/config.env` (File Manager,
or this app's Terminal) and restart the app. Note that a seeded admin counts as
an existing administrator, so the first SSO user would then be a normal user -
set it before anyone signs in only if that is the arrangement you want.

## Configuration

Settings live in `/app/data/config.env` (visible in the File Manager; `.env` in
the same directory still works, and `config.env` wins where both set a key).
The effective configuration - runtimes, ports, which auth providers are on,
whether the admin password is set - is written to `/app/data/config.txt` on
every start, so it can be read without opening a terminal.

## A note on what these runtimes do

The `js` and `py` runtimes execute the program files stored on SASjs Drive,
server-side. That is the point of the application - and it is a privilege
boundary. Anyone who can write to the Drive can run code in this container.

Keep the app behind Cloudron access control, and grant Drive write access only
to trusted authors.

## Backups

Cloudron backs up `/app/data` and the MongoDB addon, so the SASjs Drive, logs
and uploaded content are all covered. Backups are taken automatically before
every app update.

## 1.3.4

- **The configuration is readable without shell access.** Settings live in
  `/app/data/config.env` - the same `KEY=VALUE` format as before, under a
  visible name - and the effective configuration is written to
  `/app/data/config.txt` on every start. `RUN_TIMES`, the auth providers, the
  ports and whether an admin password is set are all visible there; credentials
  appear as `set`/`unset`, never by value.
- **The config file is read, not sourced.** The entrypoint runs as root and the
  data directory is writable by the application user, so executing a file from
  there would let anyone who can write to it run shell as root on the next
  restart - privilege escalation on an application whose purpose is running
  uploaded code. Only `KEY=VALUE` lines are honoured now, with `dotenv`'s
  quoting and comment rules so the entrypoint and the server agree.

## 1.3.3

- **No admin account is created unless you ask for one.** The entrypoint no
  longer generates a password into `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`. With
  `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` unset there is no local admin at all, and the FIRST
  user to sign in through Cloudron SSO becomes the administrator - which makes
  a fresh install usable without hunting for a credential in a dotfile the
  platform's File Manager does not show. Set `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` to seed a
  break-glass local admin instead; a seeded admin counts as an existing
  administrator, so the first SSO user is then a normal user.
- **`/app/data/.env` is the app's configuration file.** It is read on every
  start - by the entrypoint before its defaults, and by the server itself,
  which runs with `DATA_DIR` as its working directory - so the settings above
  can be changed from the File Manager. Cloudron's own addon credentials are
  still read from the environment at every start and are never cached here.
- Upstream: server mode no longer refuses to start without
  `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` when an external provider is enabled, because that
  provider can bootstrap the first administrator. It still fails closed when no
  provider is configured, since then no account could ever exist.

## 1.2.1

- **The Cloudron package has moved into the SASjs Server repository** as
  `container/cloudron/`, and the standalone `sasjs/server-cloudron` repository
  is deprecated. The app package now installs the same container image every
  other user runs - `ghcr.io/sasjs/server`, built and published by the
  repository's own release workflow - so the app version and the image tag
  always refer to the same commit.
- The image entrypoint is platform-neutral: outside Cloudron it is configured
  by the application's own environment variables (with `DATA_DIR` for the
  writable state). Inside Cloudron it detects the `CLOUDRON_*` addon variables
  and wires them up as before; `container/tests/verify-start-sh.sh` keeps both
  sides in sync with the manifest.
- Upstream v1.2.1: the release executables are built with node24 pkg targets,
  and the container image follows the source build on Node 24, which the OIDC
  sign-in path requires.

## 1.1.0

- Upstream v1.1.0, which adds OIDC sign-in and just-in-time provisioning.
- **Cloudron single sign-on replaces LDAP.** The `oidc` addon is declared with
  `loginRedirectUri` `/SASLogon/openid/callback`, `logoutRedirectUri`
  `/SASLogon/openid/logout` and `tokenSignatureAlgorithm` RS256; the `ldap`
  addon is gone. `start.sh` maps `CLOUDRON_OIDC_*` onto the app's `OIDC_*`
  names and builds the absolute `OIDC_REDIRECT_URI` the app requires from
  `CLOUDRON_APP_ORIGIN`. `AUTH_PROVIDERS` still defaults to SSO and an empty
  value falls back to local accounts. Note the single-dash default: `:-` would
  treat an explicitly empty value as unset and re-enable OIDC.
- **The image now builds from source instead of the `linux.zip` release
  asset.** That asset is a `pkg` binary targeting node16, which has no global
  `fetch` - and the OIDC sign-in path calls it. Against the v1.1.0 binary,
  `GET /SASLogon/openid` returns 500 (`Failed to fetch the OIDC discovery
  document ...: undefined is not a function`); the same source built on a
  modern Node completes the sign-in redirect. The Dockerfile clones the pinned
  tag, asserts the commit it resolves to, and builds the web bundle then the
  API, as upstream's own `DockerfileApi` does. Side effect: the unfixable
  findings from the pkg bundle's own Go stdlib and bundled `node_modules` are
  gone.
- `tests/verify-oidc.sh` boots the app with Cloudron-shaped OIDC configuration
  against a stub identity provider and asserts the sign-in route redirects with
  our client id, our exact redirect URI, the openid scope and a state value.
  The CI smoke job runs the same assertion against the built image.
- `tests/verify-start-sh.sh` now also asserts that `OIDC_SIGNING_ALG` matches
  the manifest's `tokenSignatureAlgorithm` and that `loginRedirectUri` matches
  the path `start.sh` builds - a mismatch fails only at sign-in, which is the
  worst place to find it.
- `tests/verify-runtimes.sh` is removed. It exercised the release asset this
  package no longer uses, and its runtime coverage (both runtimes execute) is
  in `verify-server-mode.sh` and the CI smoke job.
- The app-level harnesses take `API_BIN`, skip when no server or MongoDB is
  present, and refuse to run when something already holds their port - a stale
  process makes every assertion describe the old binary.

## 0.39.8

- Initial Cloudron package for SASjs Server v0.39.8.
- Server mode: MongoDB addon for storage, Cloudron LDAP addon for user login,
  local storage for the SASjs Drive and logs.
- Default runtimes are `js,py` (JavaScript and Python stored programs). Node
  comes from the `cloudron/node-base` image, Python 3 is installed in the
  Dockerfile, so the package needs no SAS binary.
- SAS and R remain available by adding them to `RUN_TIMES` and supplying their
  executable paths from outside the image.
- `AUTH_PROVIDERS` can be set to an empty value to disable Cloudron LDAP and
  authenticate against the local database only.
- Initial local admin password generated on first boot into
  `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`.
- CI pipeline (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`): validate, build, Trivy reports
  (full os+library table and SARIF artifact) with gates on OS packages and
  Dockerfile misconfiguration, and a server-mode smoke test against MongoDB 8
  that drives the real auth flow and executes both runtimes. The smoke job
  depends only on validate, so a scan finding cannot hide a functional failure.
- `linux-libc-dev` is pulled up to the archive's current version in the
  Dockerfile, which clears the kernel-header CVEs the OS-layer scan gate would
  otherwise flag on every build.
- start.sh creates the `/app/data` tree before writing the initial admin
  password. On Cloudron the localstorage addon always creates that directory,
  so the ordering bug was invisible there; it broke a plain `docker run` and was
  caught by the CI smoke test. The start.sh harness no longer pre-creates the
  directory, so it covers this.
- `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` is now honoured when supplied. Previously start.sh
  always overwrote it with a generated password, which is why the first CI
  smoke run failed to authenticate. Unset, behaviour is unchanged: a password
  is generated into `/app/data/.initial-admin-password`.
- `.trivyignore.yaml` records one audited exception: `DS-0002` wants a non-root
  `USER`, but Cloudron images must start as root to chown the platform-managed
  `/app/data` before dropping to the `cloudron` user via gosu.
- Manifest: `proxyAuth` puts the whole app behind Cloudron's authentication
  wall, excluding only the health-check endpoint. This replaces the VPN
  requirement: VPN gating has no manifest field (it is the per-app platform
  setting `requiresVpn`), so Cloudron auth is enforced instead.
  `supportsBearerAuth` is enabled so programmatic SASjs clients still reach the
  API through the wall.
- Manifest: `minBoxVersion` raised to 10.0.0 and `targetBoxVersion` set to
  10.0.5, the box this estate runs. `mediaLinks` is populated - Cloudron
  requires it to be non-empty to publish - with a 3:1 banner composed from the
  app's own logo, since upstream ships no screenshots.
- Manifest: `packageUrl`, needed by `cloudron versions init` when publishing.
  This is also what forces `minBoxVersion` to 10.0.0: Cloudron's loader rejects
  the manifest with "manifest.packageUrl requires minBoxVersion of atleast
  10.0.0", a cross-field rule its JSON schema does not express and so does not
  catch. `scripts/check-manifest.py` now enforces these rules - read from the
  schema's own field descriptions - and `tests/verify-manifest.sh` proves it
  reproduces that exact error, so the manifest cannot be published unloadable
  again.
- Release pipeline (`.github/workflows/release.yml`): a `v*` tag matching the
  manifest version builds the image, smoke tests it before pushing anything,
  pushes it to `ghcr.io/sasjs/server-cloudron`, records the digest in
  `CloudronVersions.json`, commits the catalogue back and creates the release.
- `scripts/update-versions.py` generates and validates `CloudronVersions.json`,
  because Cloudron's `cloudron versions add` needs the CLI and a logged-in
  workstation. It inlines `file://` text fields, keeps `icon` as a reference,
  refuses to move semver backwards, and refuses a manifest missing any field
  Cloudron requires for publishing.
- A recorded catalogue entry is refreshed whenever anything about it changes,
  not only when the image digest changes. The guard previously compared the
  image alone, so a manifest-only fix - a corrected `minBoxVersion`, say -
  would leave the catalogue serving the stale embedded manifest and installs
  would keep failing on a manifest that no longer existed in the repository.
- The smoke test moved to `.github/actions/smoke-test` so CI and the release
  workflow share one implementation.
- Manifest: `memoryLimit` set to 1 GiB. Cloudron's default is 256 MB, which
  this app exceeds - it runs Node, serves the web UI from the same process and
  spawns a `node` or `python3` child per stored program.
- Manifest: `postInstallMessage` (`file://POSTINSTALL.md`) and a `checklist`
  covering the initial admin password and the Drive-write trust boundary, plus
  `iconUrl` and `documentationUrl` for the community app listing.
- Dockerfile: `EXPOSE 5000`, matching the manifest's `httpPort`.
- `scripts/verify-installable.py` checks, using only anonymous requests, that a
  Cloudron box can actually install the package: it fetches the published
  catalogue, confirms the registry serves the exact digest the catalogue names
  (not merely an image with the right tag), and fetches every URL the dashboard
  and store will. It fails loudly if any step needs a credential, which is the
  difference between "the pipeline is green" and "a box can install this".
- Verification harnesses in `tests/`: start.sh behaviour (33 assertions),
  desktop-mode runtimes, server mode against MongoDB (9 assertions), manifest
  rules, and the catalogue generator.

manifest.description:
# SASjs Server

SASjs Server is an open-source Node.js wrapper that gives you a REST API, a
filesystem (SASjs Drive) for storing programs, execution of Stored Programs
from a URL, and web-app streaming - the same role SAS 9 Stored Processes and
Viya Jobs play.

This package runs it in **server mode**: multi-user, with Cloudron single
sign-on, and a MongoDB store.

## Runtimes: JavaScript and Python

`RUN_TIMES` defaults to `js,py`, so stored programs are JavaScript or Python.
Node and Python 3 are both in the image, which makes this package
self-contained - **no SAS binary is required**.

SAS and R can be enabled by adding them to `RUN_TIMES`, but each needs an
executable supplied from outside the image: SAS is proprietary and licensed
and cannot be redistributed, and R is not installed here.

## Addons used

- **MongoDB** - the server-mode database (users, groups, tokens, sessions).
- **OIDC** - Cloudron single sign-on. Users sign in with their Cloudron
  account, so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without
  maintaining a second account list.
- **Local storage** - `/app/data`, which holds the SASjs Drive, logs, uploads
  and the initial admin password.

## Authentication

The app sits behind Cloudron's own authentication wall, so an unauthenticated
visitor gets a Cloudron login screen rather than the application. Set this up
at install time - the `proxyAuth` addon cannot be added to an app afterwards.

Inside that wall, day-to-day logins go through Cloudron single sign-on (OIDC),
so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA. Set `AUTH_PROVIDERS` to an
empty value to skip SSO and authenticate against the local database only.

There is no pre-created admin account. The FIRST user to sign in becomes the
administrator; every user after that is a normal user, so grant the others what
they need under Settings > Permissions once you are in.

A break-glass local `admin` account is optional. To seed one, put
`ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong password>` in `/app/data/config.env` (File Manager,
or this app's Terminal) and restart the app. Note that a seeded admin counts as
an existing administrator, so the first SSO user would then be a normal user -
set it before anyone signs in only if that is the arrangement you want.

## Configuration

Settings live in `/app/data/config.env` (visible in the File Manager; `.env` in
the same directory still works, and `config.env` wins where both set a key).
The effective configuration - runtimes, ports, which auth providers are on,
whether the admin password is set - is written to `/app/data/config.txt` on
every start, so it can be read without opening a terminal.

## A note on what these runtimes do

The `js` and `py` runtimes execute the program files stored on SASjs Drive,
server-side. That is the point of the application - and it is a privilege
boundary. Anyone who can write to the Drive can run code in this container.

Keep the app behind Cloudron access control, and grant Drive write access only
to trusted authors.

## Backups

Cloudron backs up `/app/data` and the MongoDB addon, so the SASjs Drive, logs
and uploaded content are all covered. Backups are taken automatically before
every app update.

  ports and whether an admin password is set are all visible there; credentials
  appear as `set`/`unset`, never by value.

  data directory is writable by the application user, so executing a file from

  restart - privilege escalation on an application whose purpose is running
  uploaded code. Only `KEY=VALUE` lines are honoured now, with `dotenv`'s
  quoting and comment rules so the entrypoint and the server agree.

  platform's File Manager does not show. Set `ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL` to seed a
  break-glass local admin instead; a seeded admin counts as an existing
  administrator, so the first SSO user is then a normal user.

  start - by the entrypoint before its defaults, and by the server itself,
  which runs with `DATA_DIR` as its working directory - so the settings above
  can be changed from the File Manager. Cloudron's own addon credentials are
  still read from the environment at every start and are never cached here.

  provider can bootstrap the first administrator. It still fails closed when no

  sides in sync with the manifest.

  and the container image follows the source build on Node 24, which the OIDC
  sign-in path requires.

## 1.1.0

- Upstream v1.1.0, which adds OIDC sign-in and just-in-time provisioning.
- **Cloudron single sign-on replaces LDAP.** The `oidc` addon is declared with
  `loginRedirectUri` `/SASLogon/openid/callback`, `logoutRedirectUri`
  `/SASLogon/openid/logout` and `tokenSignatureAlgorithm` RS256; the `ldap`
  addon is gone. `start.sh` maps `CLOUDRON_OIDC_*` onto the app's `OIDC_*`
  names and builds the absolute `OIDC_REDIRECT_URI` the app requires from
  `CLOUDRON_APP_ORIGIN`. `AUTH_PROVIDERS` still defaults to SSO and an empty
  value falls back to local accounts. Note the single-dash default: `:-` would
  treat an explicitly empty value as unset and re-enable OIDC.

  asset.** That asset is a `pkg` binary targeting node16, which has no global
  `fetch` - and the OIDC sign-in path calls it. Against the v1.1.0 binary,
  `GET /SASLogon/openid` returns 500 (`Failed to fetch the OIDC discovery
  document ...: undefined is not a function`); the same source built on a
  modern Node completes the sign-in redirect. The Dockerfile clones the pinned
  tag, asserts the commit it resolves to, and builds the web bundle then the
  API, as upstream's own `DockerfileApi` does. Side effect: the unfixable
  findings from the pkg bundle's own Go stdlib and bundled `node_modules` are
  gone.

  against a stub identity provider and asserts the sign-in route redirects with
  our client id, our exact redirect URI, the openid scope and a state value.
  The CI smoke job runs the same assertion against the built image.

  the manifest's `tokenSignatureAlgorithm` and that `loginRedirectUri` matches
  the path `start.sh` builds - a mismatch fails only at sign-in, which is the
  worst place to find it.

  package no longer uses, and its runtime coverage (both runtimes execute) is
  in `verify-server-mode.sh` and the CI smoke job.
- The app-level harnesses take `API_BIN`, skip when no server or MongoDB is
  present, and refuse to run when something already holds their port - a stale
  process makes every assertion describe the old binary.

manifest.description:
# SASjs Server

SASjs Server is an open-source Node.js wrapper that gives you a REST API, a
filesystem (SASjs Drive) for storing programs, execution of Stored Programs
from a URL, and web-app streaming - the same role SAS 9 Stored Processes and
Viya Jobs play.

This package runs it in **server mode**: multi-user, with Cloudron single
sign-on, and a MongoDB store.

## Runtimes: JavaScript and Python

`RUN_TIMES` defaults to `js,py`, so stored programs are JavaScript or Python.
Node and Python 3 are both in the image, which makes this package
self-contained - **no SAS binary is required**.

SAS and R can be enabled by adding them to `RUN_TIMES`, but each needs an
executable supplied from outside the image: SAS is proprietary and licensed
and cannot be redistributed, and R is not installed here.

## Addons used

- **MongoDB** - the server-mode database (users, groups, tokens, sessions).
- **OIDC** - Cloudron single sign-on. Users sign in with their Cloudron
  account, so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without
  maintaining a second account list.
- **Local storage** - `/app/data`, which holds the SASjs Drive, logs, uploads
  and the initial admin password.

## Authentication

The app sits behind Cloudron's own authentication wall, so an unauthenticated
visitor gets a Cloudron login screen rather than the application. Set this up
at install time - the `proxyAuth` addon cannot be added to an app afterwards.

Inside that wall, day-to-day logins go through Cloudron single sign-on (OIDC),
so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA. Set `AUTH_PROVIDERS` to an
empty value to skip SSO and authenticate against the local database only.

There is no pre-created admin account. The FIRST user to sign in becomes the
administrator; every user after that is a normal user, so grant the others what
they need under Settings > Permissions once you are in.

A break-glass local `admin` account is optional. To seed one, put
`ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong password>` in `/app/data/config.env` (File Manager,
or this app's Terminal) and restart the app. Note that a seeded admin counts as
an existing administrator, so the first SSO user would then be a normal user -
set it before anyone signs in only if that is the arrangement you want.

## Configuration

Settings live in `/app/data/config.env` (visible in the File Manager; `.env` in
the same directory still works, and `config.env` wins where both set a key).
The effective configuration - runtimes, ports, which auth providers are on,
whether the admin password is set - is written to `/app/data/config.txt` on
every start, so it can be read without opening a terminal.

## A note on what these runtimes do

The `js` and `py` runtimes execute the program files stored on SASjs Drive,
server-side. That is the point of the application - and it is a privilege
boundary. Anyone who can write to the Drive can run code in this container.

Keep the app behind Cloudron access control, and grant Drive write access only
to trusted authors.

## Backups

Cloudron backs up `/app/data` and the MongoDB addon, so the SASjs Drive, logs
and uploaded content are all covered. Backups are taken automatically before
every app update.

  account, so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA without
  maintaining a second account list.
- **Local storage** - `/app/data`, which holds the SASjs Drive, logs, uploads
  and the initial admin password.

## Authentication

The app sits behind Cloudron's own authentication wall, so an unauthenticated
visitor gets a Cloudron login screen rather than the application. Set this up
at install time - the `proxyAuth` addon cannot be added to an app afterwards.

Inside that wall, day-to-day logins go through Cloudron single sign-on (OIDC),
so access follows Cloudron users, groups and MFA. Set `AUTH_PROVIDERS` to an
empty value to skip SSO and authenticate against the local database only.

There is no pre-created admin account. The FIRST user to sign in becomes the
administrator; every user after that is a normal user, so grant the others what
they need under Settings > Permissions once you are in.

set it before anyone signs in only if that is the arrangement you want.

Password sign-in for local (database) accounts can be closed off entirely: set
`LOCAL_LOGIN_ENABLED=false` in `/app/data/config.env` and a local account cannot
sign in at all, while Cloudron single sign-on and LDAP keep working. This
package's `proxyAuth` addon sets `supportsBearerAuth: true`, which programmatic

the following users and groups". A Cloudron install is unrestricted by default,

uploaded to SASjs Drive. Unrestricted, both go to every user on the Cloudron.

  which runs with `DATA_DIR` as its working directory - so the settings above

  provider can bootstrap the first administrator. It still fails closed when no
  provider is configured, since then no account could ever exist.

  by the application's own environment variables (with `DATA_DIR` for the
  writable state). Inside Cloudron it detects the `CLOUDRON_*` addon variables
  and wires them up as before; `container/tests/verify-start-sh.sh` keeps both
  sides in sync with the manifest.

  and the container image follows the source build on Node 24, which the OIDC
  sign-in path requires.

- **Cloudron single sign-on replaces LDAP.** The `oidc` addon is declared with

  `/SASLogon/openid/logout` and `tokenSignatureAlgorithm` RS256; the `ldap`
  addon is gone. `start.sh` maps `CLOUDRON_OIDC_*` onto the app's `OIDC_*`
  names and builds the absolute `OIDC_REDIRECT_URI` the app requires from

  value falls back to local accounts. Note the single-dash default: `:-` would
